COWEN: Are you familiar with Greg Clark’s  hypotheses and economic history that the
English in particular, possibly also the  Dutch, that they interbred themselves
into lower rates of time preference, more  savings, more investment, more patience,
and that that’s why the Industrial Revolution  came to England? Do you have a view on that?
DIAMOND: Why did the Industrial Revolution come  to England? England is an island. England did not
need standing armies, England did not constantly  get invaded. In fact, the last successful
invasion of England was 1066. England being  an island allowed England not to need an army,
gradually to develop democracy. Democracy  is a productive form of government. Also,
England is on the Atlantic coast. England and  the Netherlands, and for Spain and Portugal,
they were the countries that spread around the  world because they were on the Atlantic coast.
Also, Spain was on the Mediterranean,  but the Mediterranean was the testing
ground for developing ships and navigation  that were then used across the Atlantic.
I’d say that it was geography that  accounts for England’s predominance.
COWEN: Deirdre McCloskey attributes the  differences to ideology, individualism, ideas of
liberty, enlightenment, and maybe to some extent,  Christianity. What do you think of her work?
DIAMOND: I don’t know her work, but the idea  that it has to do with the Enlightenment, that’s
related to what I was just telling you, that in  the case of England, not having an army meant
that England could develop a democracy. It was  in the 1600s that England chopped off the head of
its king, and then parliament became powerful in  England. Democracy, as Winston Churchill said, is
the worst form of government except for all other  forms of government that have been tried. With
democracy, you can suggest an idea, and there’s  not a dictator who will tell you to shut up.
Also, in the case of Netherlands, why did the  Industrial Revolution begin first in England?
Democracy didn’t have a standing army, and  why did it next spread to the Netherlands?
Probably because the Netherlands faces England,  but also the Netherlands was a democracy early.
COWEN: Do you have a view on the historical  theories of Daron Acemoglu that it’s fundamentally
about whether or not you have extractive  institutions versus inclusive institutions?
DIAMOND: Yes, I do know Daron and Jim  Robinson, who shared the Nobel Prize together,
particularly Jim Robinson. I’ve had more to do  with Jim Robinson. I’ve learned more from Jim
Robinson in the last 20 years than from any  other individual. It was Jim who taught me
the power of natural experiments. My career  was as a laboratory scientist, as a gallbladder
scientist, who did manipulative experiments in the  laboratory. On people, we can’t do manipulative
experiments. We can’t go around experimentally  killing people and seeing what happens.
In my work in New Guinea studying New Guinea  birds, I can’t go around exterminating New
Guinea birds. I had to develop techniques of  natural experiments, comparing mountains that
did or did not have a leading bird species.  My natural experiments were relatively crude.
Jim Robinson and Daron are masters of natural  experiments. My current book on leaders uses
natural experiments to ask questions about  political leaders, then business leaders,
and sports coaches. I admire Daron and Jim a lot.  I think that they give less credit to geography
and more credit to institutions than I do, but  they are great scientists and great writers.
COWEN: Now your book on environmental Collapse,
that one seemed too pessimistic to me.  Have you become more optimistic since then?
DIAMOND: In some ways, yes. I’m more optimistic  now than I was 20 years ago. One might say,
for heaven’s sake, why? Because now there are  more people, we have more destructive power,
and there’s less time left before we risk  going over the cliff. In the last 20 years,
there have been two developments that make  me cautiously optimistic. One is what has
happened in the world of big businesses. Twenty  years ago, I would have said that the most evil,
destructive forces in the world are big  businesses. It was true that 20 years ago,
big businesses, for the most part, were  not much interested in the environment.
Within the last 20 years, big businesses have  been increasingly interested in the environment;
Walmart, for example. Walmart has taken  a lead in sustainable products. Unilever
has taken a lead in sustainable fishery. Even oil  companies. I was sent out by World Wildlife Fund
in 1999 to do environmental studies in the oil  fields that Chevron managed in Papua New Guinea.
I went out expecting that they would be awful.  I learned, in fact, that Chevron is and was
ultra-cautious in the oil fields because they  knew that if they made a mess, New Guineans would
sue them. If they made a mess, they would not get  contracts for developing the Norwegian oil fields.
One thing that makes me optimistic is that  I’ve learned that at least some big companies
care a lot about the environment. The  other thing that makes me optimistic
is the increased role of young people. Twenty-five  years ago, young people were not much interested
in the environment. Now they’ve got a lot  interested in the environment. My own son,
at age five and six, I remember them  and their class at age six, marching
to make a plea for protecting the  rainforest. I’m cautiously optimistic.
I would say the chances are 51 percent that we  will have a good outcome and only 49 percent that
we will have a bad outcome. I’m more optimistic  now than I was 20 years ago, particularly for
those two reasons: the development of  environmental concerns among some big
businesses and the much more increased interest of  young people in the environment and in our future.
COWEN: Are you more optimistic about Australia?
Won’t water desalination just  solve their major problems?
DIAMOND: Water desalination requires energy.
COWEN: They have solar energy, right?  Batteries will get better. Maybe it costs
them 2 percent of GDP. That’s one year’s  growth. They give up a year’s growth,
and they have all the water they need.
DIAMOND: We shall see. It has not happened  yet. Fortunately, there is development of
sustainable forms of energy, particularly wind  energy and solar energy, which now account for,
what, 10 percent or 15 percent of energy  production in the United States. Nuclear
energy: About 85 percent or 90 percent of the  energy in France comes from nuclear energy.
There’s work on getting energy from tides. There’s
work on getting energy geothermally  from heat in the ground. We shall see.
COWEN: What do you think is the single  biggest environmental problem at the macro
level for the world? Is it climate change? Is it  biodiversity? Is it water? Is it something else?
DIAMOND: I’m laughing because welcome  to why interviewers find interviewing
Jared Diamond so frustrating. When  they ask me a question, “What is the
single most important thing?” My answer is  always the single most important thing is
not to look for the single most important  thing, because the world is complicated.
When a couple who are about to get married asks  me, “What is the single most important thing
for happy marriage?” My answer is the single most  important thing is not to look for the single most
important thing. Because for a happy marriage, you  need to get 37 things right. If you get 36 things
right, and you disagree about sex or you disagree  about religion, the marriage will fall apart.
To go to your question, what is the most  important thing in the world today? There
are many things that we have to get right. The  most important things that we have to get right
are climate change, inequality, and the nuclear  risk, the risk that we will have nuclear war
and that we will have nuclear winter. I didn’t  give you one answer, but I gave you three answers.
COWEN: Do you have ideas on what we  should do to limit nuclear war risk?
DIAMOND: What should we do to limit  nuclear war risk? Yes, conversations. Sure,
it’s obvious. Conversations between the countries  that have nuclear weapons. There have been such
conversations. After the Cuban Missile Crisis,  Russia and the United States had uninterrupted
conversations because Russia and the United States  saw how close we had come to blowing up the world.
China and the United States have not come that  far, but we’re at least having conversations.
The big danger player today  is, of course, North Korea.
Our current president has made an effort and  now says that he’s going to make another effort
to get conversations going with North Korea. In  short, my answer to your question, what do we
need to avoid a nuclear war? Conversations among  the nine countries that have nuclear weapons.
COWEN: Do you still type using  the Dvorak keyboard layout?
DIAMOND: I’m pausing here. I’m  looking at my wife’s computer here,
which is the Dvorak keyboard. I would say that  we’re invested in the Dvorak keyboard. Yes,
another keyboard would be much more  efficient, but we’ve got the Dvorak
keyboard, so I don’t see any movement  toward replacing the Dvorak keyboard.
COWEN: Do you think there’s too much  inertia in the world of standards then?
DIAMOND: I wouldn’t say it’s inertia. I would  say we just got too much investment in the
Dvorak keyboard. Young people learn  how to use the Dvorak keyboard. Yes,
another keyboard would be more efficient, but  they learn the Dvorak keyboard, and it works.
There are other things that they care about  rather than getting a different keyboard.
COWEN: Where’s your favorite  place to go birdwatching?
DIAMOND: My favorite place to go birdwatching  is the street where I live in Los Angeles,
Stone Canyon Road. My list of species for  my street is 189 species. I go birdwatching
on my street every Saturday and every Sunday.  That’s my favorite place to go birdwatching in
the United States. Of course, my favorite place  to go birdwatching in the world is New Guinea,
no close second. New Guinea has the birds of  paradise, the world’s most beautiful birds.
New Guinea has bowerbirds, the animals  that build the most complex structures
other than us humans. The bower  of a bowerbird—a bird this size,
about the size of a jay—a male builds a bower  that may be nine feet tall and is decorated
with hundreds of blue fruits and red flowers  and orange mushrooms. It has dozens and dozens
of pans of stuff, of shells, of pandanus  leaves. Once you’ve been to New Guinea,
the rest of the world is boring. That’s the  only disadvantage of being in New Guinea.
COWEN: Panama, Costa Rica, Santa Marta,  Colombia, are they worth going to for birds?
DIAMOND: They’re worth going to,  but they’re second to New Guinea.
COWEN: Now, you’ve written quite a fair number of  books that one could call big picture or big idea
books. In terms of your method, how does each one  come about? An idea comes to you in the shower,
or you start writing out many ideas, and you  abandon most of them? What would you say is your
method for a thing that you do and very few people  have done in the quantity that you’ve done it?
DIAMOND: Well, I’m interested in lots  of things. I’m interested in languages,
genetics, human evolution. It means that  until the 1980s, I was the world’s expert on
the gallbladder. Then my twin sons were born. Our  twin sons were born in the year 1987. I realized
that the future of my twin sons was not going  to depend upon gallbladders. It was going to
depend upon history and geography. There were  many major questions in history and geography.
My first book, The Third Chimpanzee, had chapters  on things that then ended up in other books.
One chapter of my book, The Third Chimpanzee,  my book from 1991, got expanded into Guns,
Germs, and Steel. Another chapter  of my book, The Third Chimpanzee,
got expanded into Collapse. Still another chapter  got expanded into Why Is Sex Fun? My current book
about leaders is a subject that has interested  me for a long time as a result of being born
in 1937 and growing up in the shadow of  Hitler and wondering whether World War
II and the Holocaust would have achieved the  form they did if it hadn’t been for Hitler.
COWEN: What’s your most unusual successful work
habit? You get a lot done, right? You’re  extremely productive in multiple areas.
DIAMOND: Do I have a single unusual work habit?  Once again, welcome to Jared. No, I don’t have
one work habit. My work habits are that I’m  comfortable sitting down at a desk and working
at the desk. I’ve learned to take off time in  the evening instead of working on my book in the
evening. In the evening now, I listen to music,  the composer, Johann Sebastian Bach. I’ve sung.
I play the piano. I play the organ. I play the  viola. Bach wrote 200 cantatas. I’ve been telling
myself—I sang in 20 of them—I would like to get  to know all Bach cantatas. A year and a half ago,
the time arrived. I’m now going to listen to  Bach cantatas at the rate of one per week. I’m
now up to cantata number 57. It means that in the  evening, I’m relaxed and I’m not fretting. I’m not
wasting my time getting anxious. I’m instead  listening to Bach cantatas. I get good sleep.
COWEN: Are you listening to the Suzuki recordings  or the Harnoncourt, or which ones? Gardiner?
DIAMOND: I have three recordings. Gardiner is  one. Although I listen to them every night,
I can tell you Gardiner, but I can’t  tell you the names of the other Bach
cantata recordings that I listen to  every night. I just listen to them.
COWEN: We once had Suzuki  on as a guest. He was great.
Your father, Louis Diamond,  he was a great benefactor
in hematology. How did that shape your life?
DIAMOND: My father and my mother shaped  my life. They were different people.
Dad was a hematologist and a pediatrician, a  children’s doctor. The result was that growing up,
whenever people asked me, “What do you want  to do when you grow up?” My answer was,
“I want to be a doctor like my father.” Dad also  did scientific research. When I went to college,
initially, I was pre-med. I thought I would be a  doctor like my father. Then I realized that what
really interests me is science, including  medical science. I went into physiology,
which is a medical science. Dad  shaped my career in that direction.
My mother was a linguist and a teacher. Mom  taught me to read when I was three years old.
When I started learning languages in school, my  first language was Latin. I didn’t realize that
it was my first foreign language. I didn’t realize  that you had to learn grammar. I just memorized
vocabulary. After a month, I was way out of shape  with Latin because I hadn’t learned the grammar.
My mother then sat down with me every night for a  year, and we went through my Latin lessons. From
Mom, I developed my love of languages. Mom was a  concert pianist, so I developed my love of music.
I gained different things from Mom—languages and  music particularly—and from my father, science.
COWEN: Do you think your own  shift away from studying the
gallbladder shaped the lives of your children?
DIAMOND: Yes, not because I taught them not  to study gallbladders, but because the birth
of my children made me realize that I better  do something more important for the world than
studying gallbladder. In fact, I’m an optimistic  person. I don’t get depressed, usually. The one
time in my life that I was depressed for a week  was when I learned that I was awarded one of these
MacArthur Fellowships, the so-called genius  awards. When I got the MacArthur Fellowship,
I thought I would have been excited. Instead,  I was depressed for a week. Why? Because the
